\begin{abstract}
\noindent
Personal knowledge-management artifacts accumulate faster than they are
validated, and a reader who trusts a study note inherits its defects
silently. This paper treats one such artifact as an object of assessment
rather than as an authority. A case-insensitive recursive search of the
author's Obsidian vault localized exactly one candidate: a CompTIA
Security+ textbook by Mark Ciampa, retained both as a source PDF and as a
directory of fifteen extracted per-module notes. Scope was narrowed to
Module 7, \emph{Identity and Access Management} (SY0-701), which was read
in full at 471 lines and is organized around three objectives:
authentication credential types, authentication best practices, and access
control schemes. A line-level audit exposed three defects in the note,
including an internal contradiction on password expiry and a review item
presenting two textually identical answer options. A 25-item examination
protocol was then administered, each item carrying a nominal value of four
points, under a requirement that every answer be scored and carry a
line-level citation into the source. The supplied answer key failed an
internal-consistency check: in roughly three quarters of its entries the
printed option letter contradicted the printed explanatory rationale, and
several entries were topically unrelated to any supplied item. Subject-matter
re-mapping established that the rationales were reliable while the letters
had been displaced; reissuing the same items with intra-question option
reordering rendered the key internally consistent throughout, confirming
displacement without resolving its cause. Rescoring against the aligned key
yielded three accuracy figures under two weighting schemes: 72\pct\ under
strict all-or-nothing scoring, 81\pct\ under selection-weighted scoring of
multi-select items, and 86\pct\ under strict scoring with the four items
judged defective or disputed excluded. Decomposition revealed marked
heterogeneity: the five items newly introduced by the reissued set were
answered without exception, while the twenty carried-over items yielded
thirteen correct, with failure concentrated where the source note is silent
on the distinction under test.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} study-material assessment; assessment validity;
answer-key misalignment; access control; authentication; knowledge
management.

\bigskip
\noindent\textbf{Scope note.} This is a single-artifact, single-analyst
study-material assessment. No external literature was consulted. All
references are internal artifacts. Quantitative claims are derived
arithmetic from the session record; none have been extrapolated beyond the
population actually observed.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\subsection{Motivation}

A study note is a lossy derivative of a source text, and the lossy steps
that produce it are rarely recorded. When such a note is later mined for
examination practice, three questions become simultaneously live: does the
note state what the source states, is the practice material answerable
against the note at all, and can the score attached to the attempt be
trusted? The third question is the one most often skipped. A score is
ordinarily reported as a number, and a number launders whatever corruption
sat upstream of it.

The case reported here is a compact instance of precisely that failure mode.
An answer key was supplied with an examination set. The key was internally
contradictory --- the letter it marked was not the option its own
explanation defended --- and the contradiction was not subtle. It was
detectable by reading the key against itself, without reference to any
subject-matter expertise. Despite that, a score had already been produced
from it. The purpose of this paper is to document the detection, the
reconstruction, the rescoring, and the residue that reconstruction could not
remove.

\subsection{Research questions}

\begin{itemize}[label={RQ\arabic*.}]
\item What structural and factual defects does a line-level audit of the
      Module~7 note expose, and are they mutually independent?
\item Can a supplied answer key be validated for internal consistency, and
      what is the recoverable structure of a key that fails that
      validation?
\item What accuracy does the analyst achieve against the reconstructed key
      under each of three scoring weightings, and do the figures
      reconcile?
\item How is that accuracy distributed across item provenance, and does it
      track the note's explicitness on the distinction each item actually
      tests?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Contributions}

The contribution is not a general claim about study materials. It is a
worked record of one note, one item set, one defective key, and a
reconstruction, reported with the unresolved threads left visible. Two
findings survive the reconstruction and are stated as open rather than
closed: the defects in the note itself, and the cause of the letter
displacement.

\section{Materials and Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Artifact localization}

The session opened with a request to locate a CompTIA study book within the
personal Obsidian vault. A case-insensitive recursive search was executed
over the vault. The search returned exactly one matching title.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Properties of the located artifact.}
\label{tab:artifact}
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\bfseries}p{0.36\textwidth}p{0.56\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Property & Value \\
\midrule
Matching titles returned & 1 \\
Author / exam code        & Mark Ciampa; SY0-701 \\
Stored representations    & Source PDF \emph{and} directory of extracted notes \\
Number of extracted notes & 15 (one per module) \\
Module selected           & Module 7, \emph{Identity and Access Management} \\
Length of selected note   & 471 lines, read in full \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

A single title is a useful result in itself. The search space of a
long-lived personal vault is not small, and a duplicate-across-formats
situation (one PDF, fifteen derived notes) is a common failure mode for
citation: a reader may cite the PDF for a claim that only the derived note
makes. The protocol below therefore requires that every scored answer be
anchored to a line in the \emph{module note}, not to the PDF, so that the
artifact actually being tested is the artifact being scored.

\subsection{Scope selection}

The user narrowed scope to Module~7. The note is organized around three
stated objectives, which partition the item space and give the assessment a
defensible coverage target.

\label{tab:objectives}

\toprule
\# & Objective & Assessed by items on \\
\midrule
O1 & Authentication credential types        & Knowledge factors; credential modalities \\
O2 & Authentication best practices          & Password hygiene; breach-response procedure \\
O3 & Access control schemes                 & Mandatory, discretionary, role-based \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Note audit}

A line-level audit was performed on the 471-line note prior to item
administration. Its purpose was to establish whether the note is a sound
basis for scoring at all --- a precondition for RQ2 and RQ3, since an
unsound basis invalidates any score computed against it. The audit found
three defects, recorded in Table~\ref{tab:defects} and preserved verbatim
as findings.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Defects surfaced by the line-level audit.}
\label{tab:defects}
\begin{tabular}{@{}clp{0.62\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
ID & Type & Description \\
\midrule
D1 & Contradiction &
The note states the prevailing industry practice on password expiry
\emph{and} separately issues an explicit recommendation against expiry.
A reader cannot satisfy both. \\
D2 & Malformed item &
A review question presents two answer options that are textually
identical, making the item unanswerable as written. \\
D3 & Unsatisfiable item &
An item demands two selections, but only one is supportable from the
source. The second required selection has no referent in the note. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The three defects are of different kinds and should not be treated as one
class. D1 is a \emph{content} defect: the note is internally inconsistent
about a fact, so a reader who studies it may learn either position depending
on which passage they encounter. D2 is a \emph{formatting} defect: the item
is well-formed in intent but has a degenerate option list, so a correct
reader and an incorrect reader are indistinguishable. D3 is a
\emph{coverage} defect: the note is silent on a distinction the item tests,
so the item is unanswerable from the assigned material regardless of reader
expertise. This distinction matters in \S\ref{sec:discussion}, where D3
resurfaces as the mechanism behind the observed failure cluster.

No correction to the note is reported in the session record, and none is
claimed here. Whether D1--D3 originated in the extraction of the PDF into
per-module notes, or were present in the source textbook, is not
established by the record.

\subsection{Item set and scoring protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

Twenty-five examination items were administered. Each item carried a nominal
value of four points, giving a nominal total of
$25 \times 4 = 100$ points. The protocol imposed two requirements on the
analyst:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{P\arabic*.}]
\item every item is scored --- no item may be skipped, including items the
      analyst believes are defective;
\item every scored answer carries a line-level citation into the module note.
\end{enumerate}

Requirement P1 is what makes the audit findings actionable: an unscoreable
item must be scored as incorrect or partial and flagged, not silently
dropped. Requirement P2 makes the artifact, rather than the analyst's
recall, the authority for correctness --- and it is precisely this property
that later allowed the note's silences to be localized (\S\ref{sec:local}).

\subsection{Key alignment procedure}
\label{sec:alignment}

An answer key was supplied alongside the item set. It failed an
internal-consistency check applied before any scoring was attempted. The
check requires no subject-matter knowledge: for each entry, the option letter
that the key marks as correct must be the option that the key's own
explanatory sentence defends. Two failure modes were observed.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{F\arabic*.}]
\item \emph{Letter--rationale contradiction.} In roughly three quarters of
      the key's entries, the marked letter and the written rationale
      pointed at different options.
\item \emph{Topical orphaning.} Several entries were topically unrelated to
      any supplied item --- they could not be assigned to a question at all.
\end{enumerate}

% TODO: The session records the proportion for F1 as "roughly three
% quarters" without an exact count. No integer numerator is asserted here.
% If a precise count is recovered it should replace the qualitative
% statement in F1.

The recovery procedure was a subject-matter re-mapping: for each entry, the
rationale was read on its own terms and matched to the option it actually
defends, independent of the letter printed beside it. The outcome was
asymmetric and informative --- the rationales were reliable, the letters
were not. The key therefore possessed a correct layer (prose) and a
displaced layer (labels), which is recoverable in principle: re-deriving the
letter from the rationale reconstructs the key.

To test whether the displacement was a property of the key or an artifact of
the item set's option ordering, the user reissued the same twenty-five items
with all options reordered within each question. Against the reordered set,
the key was internally consistent throughout. This confirms displacement
\emph{relative to a particular option ordering}; it does not establish the
mechanism that produced the displacement. No further cause is identified in
the record, and none is asserted here.

\subsection{Scoring schemes}
\label{sec:scoring}

Three accuracy figures were produced, under two weighting schemes. They are
defined before reporting so that each is independently checkable.

\begin{description}[style=nextline,leftmargin=0pt]
\item[W1 --- Strict, all-or-nothing.] Every item is either correct or not.
      An item answered with a correct but incomplete set of selections is
      recorded as \emph{partial} and earns no credit. Denominator is all
      25 items.
\item[W2 --- Selection-weighted.] Single-select items retain W1 treatment.
      Each multi-select item is credited proportionally to the fraction of
      its required selections that were correctly made, so an item
      requiring $k$ selections and earning $m \leq k$ correct selections
      contributes $4m/k$ of its 4 points.
\item[W3 --- Strict, restricted.] W1 applied to the 21 items remaining after
      excluding the four items judged defective or disputed by either the
      source note or the key. Denominator is 21.
\end{description}

W3 is reported because the exclusions are not neutral with respect to
difficulty: three of them correspond to the audit defects of
Table~\ref{tab:defects}, and the fourth is disputed by the key. W1 and W3
are therefore bounds of a kind --- W1 includes material the study artifact
cannot support, W3 excludes it --- and the gap between them is an
information-content quantity, not a correction.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Audit outcome}

The audit produced exactly the three defects of Table~\ref{tab:defects} and
no others. No defect of type D2 (degenerate option list) or D3
(unsupportable selection) was found among the twenty-five administered items;
the D2 and D3 instances are defects of the note's own review questions, not
of the assessment items. The administered items are, in this respect,
cleaner than the source they were drawn from.

\subsection{Key alignment outcome}

Both failure modes F1 and F2 were confirmed and then repaired by
re-derivation. The reconstructed key --- the rationales with letters
recomputed from them --- was used as the sole scoring authority for all
figures in \S\ref{sec:accuracy}. The residual, and it is a real one, is
that the cause of the displacement remains unestablished. The
option-reordering test narrows the hypothesis space without closing it: it
demonstrates that the rationales index the correct \emph{content}, and that
the letters indexed a \emph{particular ordering} that the reissued set did
not reproduce. It does not identify the process that attached those letters.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Validation of the supplied answer key.}
\label{tab:keycheck}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.42\textwidth}p{0.14\textwidth}p{0.36\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Check & Outcome & Interpretation \\
\midrule
Letter matches rationale & Fail & Present in roughly three quarters of entries \\
Entry topically matches an item & Fail & Several entries unassignable \\
Subject-matter re-mapping & Rationales valid &
Content layer intact; label layer not \\
Reissue with options reordered & Consistent throughout &
Displacement confirmed; cause unresolved \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Aggregate accuracy under three weightings}
\label{sec:accuracy}

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} reports the three figures. All three are derived
from a single underlying tally and are therefore mutually constraining; the
arithmetic is recomputed in \S\ref{sec:appendix}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Accuracy against the aligned key under three weightings.}
\label{tab:accuracy}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrl@{}}
\toprule
Scheme & Correct & Denominator & Accuracy & Note \\
\midrule
W1 Strict & 18 & 25 & 72.0\pct & 4 incorrect, 3 partial (no credit) \\
W2 Selection-weighted & --- & 25 & 81.0\pct & 20.25 points equivalent \\
W3 Strict, restricted & 18 & 21 & 85.7\pct\ $\approx$ 86\pct & 4 items excluded \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Three reconciliations hold across the three schemes, and their consistency
is the strongest evidence that the figures describe one underlying response
pattern rather than three independent tallies.

\begin{itemize}
\item $18/25 = 72.0\pct$, exact.
\item $18/21 = 85.7\pct$, which rounds to the reported 86\pct\ under W3.
      This requires that all four excluded items fell among the seven
      non-correct items; that is consistent with the reported figure, and it
      is the only allocation that yields it.
\item $20.25/25 = 81.0\pct$ under W2, implying $2.25$ fractional points
      distributed across the three partial items. The per-item fractions
      were not retained in the session record, so the \emph{distribution}
      of that credit is not recoverable here --- only its total.
\end{itemize}

The spread from 72\pct\ to 86\pct\ is fourteen points on a 100-point
nominal scale, arising entirely from scoring policy and item eligibility
rather than from any change in the analyst's responses. This is the
practical hazard the case illustrates: the same response set yields three
defensible accuracies, and the choice among them is not neutral reporting.

\subsection{Decomposition by item provenance}
\label{sec:decomposition}

The reissued set contained the same twenty-five items with reordered
options, of which five were newly introduced. This is an accidental but
usable natural split. The five new items were answered before the analyst
had encountered them; the twenty carried-over items were items on which the
analyst had already anchored during the earlier attempt.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Strict accuracy split by item provenance.}
\label{tab:provenance}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
Provenance & Items & Correct & Accuracy \\
\midrule
Newly introduced (reissued set only) & 5 & 5 & 100.0\pct \\
Carried over from earlier set       & 20 & 13 & 65.0\pct \\
\midrule
All items & 25 & 18 & 72.0\pct \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The split reconciles exactly: $5 + 13 = 18$, the W1 correct count. The
thirty-five-point gap between the two strata is the largest single effect
in the study, and it runs in a direction that must be interpreted with care.
It is \emph{not} evidence that the new items were easier in the abstract. The
five new items are, by the report, drawn from the same note and the same
three objectives.

\subsection{What the five new items test}

The five items answered without exception cover, in the order reported:
a response to a suspected multi-factor fatigue attack; digest comparison as
protection of a banking credential; the coexistence of mandatory integrity
control with discretionary access control; justification logging together
with session revocation for privileged access; and the access control
scheme whose characteristic weakness is that executed programs inherit the
account holder's privileges.

Read against the failure cluster in the next subsection, this list is
diagnostic. Each of the five tests a \emph{relational} or
\emph{procedural} property --- what to do when an attack is suspected, what a
digest comparison defends, which controls may co-exist, what a privileged
session must log and revoke, what a weakness consists of. Each is
answerable from a note that states the relevant principle, whether or not
the note enumerates it as a review topic.

\subsection{Localization of failures}
\label{sec:local}

The degradation among the carried-over items was not uniform. It was
concentrated in items where the source note is \emph{silent} on the
distinction the item tests. Three such items are named explicitly in the
record:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{S\arabic*.}]
\item precomputed hash databases --- a distinction the note does not draw;
\item the goal of \emph{using} rather than creating a password mask --- a
      distinction the note does not draw;
\item whether a hardware security key transmits authentication codes --- a
      distinction the note does not draw.
\end{enumerate}

These are all instances of defect class D3. The item is well-formed, the
option set is well-formed, and the key is aligned; the failure is that the
assigned artifact contains no proposition from which the answer can be
derived. An examinee who knows the subject matter and an examinee who has
read the note are in the same position, which is to say no position. This is
the mechanism that reconciles the two strata: where the note is explicit,
accuracy is near total, and where the note is silent, the note cannot
distinguish knowledge from recall of nothing.

Crucially, the two success strata are not disjoint from the two failure
strata by provenance. Carried-over items that test propositions the note
states explicitly were answered correctly. New items that test relations the
note states were answered correctly. What predicts failure is silence, not
novelty --- although novelty and exposure are themselves confounded in this
design, as discussed next.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{The note is sufficient, not complete}

The central substantive finding is that Module~7 performs as a
\emph{sufficient} but not a \emph{complete} basis for assessment. Sufficiency
here means that for a proposition the note states, a reader who studies the
note can answer correctly --- the correlation between explicitness and
accuracy is strong enough that failure is rare. Completeness would mean that
every proposition an item can test is present in the note; it is not, and the
three S-class failures are the direct evidence.

This has a practical consequence for extraction pipelines. A note derived
from a textbook by summarization inherits the textbook's coverage only to
the extent that the summarizer preserved it. Coverage loss is silent,
because a reader cannot detect the absence of a proposition --- only its
absence of benefit. D3 is the observable residue of that loss, and it would
not have been visible in this study without the line-level citation
requirement P2.

\subsection{Contamination and its direction}

The thirty-five-point gap in Table~\ref{tab:provenance} cannot be read as a
clean measure of item difficulty. The five new items were administered to an
analyst who had just completed a full pass of the same note, and who had
just been alerted --- by the audit --- to the note's failure modes. The
twenty carried-over items were answered after that analyst had already
anchored on them during the earlier attempt. Novelty, exposure count, and
prior commitment to a specific option all separate these strata
simultaneously, and the design does not permit them to be separated.

The honest reading is therefore directional rather than quantitative: the
new items are consistent with a study effect, and the carried-over items
with a commitment effect, and this study cannot apportion between them. What
can be said is that neither stratum produced the S-class failure pattern ---
the silent-distinction failures occurred among items whose content the note
never supplied, which is a fact about the artifact and not about the
analyst's state.

\subsection{Open findings}

Two threads survive the reconstruction and are recorded here as open rather
than closed.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{The note's defects are unrepaired.} D1, D2, and D3 were
      identified; no correction is recorded. D1 in particular is a live
      hazard: a reader who meets the industry-practice statement and the
      anti-expiry recommendation in either order may learn a different
      answer depending on which they retain.
\item \textbf{The letter displacement has no established cause.} The
      reordering test confirmed displacement and localized it to option
      ordering. Whether the letters were carried over from a different
      ordering of the same items, transcribed from a key built for a
      different set, or corrupted by a mechanical pass, is not determined
      by the record. No mechanism is proposed here.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Implications for assessment practice}

Three transferable practices follow, each of a different scope.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Validate a key against itself before using it.} The
      letter--rationale check requires no subject-matter expertise and
      detected a corruption that had already produced a score. It should
      precede, not follow, scoring.
\item \emph{Score defective items, then report both denominators.} Protocol
      P1 combined with W1 and W3 makes the cost of artifact quality
      visible as a fourteen-point spread instead of hiding it inside a
      single number.
\item \emph{Cite the artifact, not recall.} The line-level citation
      requirement is what made the S-class localization possible. Without
      it, those seven non-correct items would have been indistinguishable
      from ordinary errors.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

A single CompTIA Security+ module note was assessed end to end. The note
(471 lines, three objectives, drawn from a vault holding one PDF and
fifteen derived module notes) contains three defects spanning content,
formatting, and coverage. A 25-item, 100-point protocol with mandatory
line-level citation was administered against it. The supplied answer key was
internally inconsistent in roughly three quarters of its entries and was
reconstructed by subject-matter re-mapping of its rationales; reissue of the
items under a new option ordering confirmed the displacement while leaving
its cause open.

Against the aligned key, accuracy was 72\pct\ under strict all-or-nothing
scoring, 81\pct\ under selection-weighted scoring, and 86\pct\ under strict
scoring with defective and disputed items excluded --- three figures
reconciling to a single tally. Decomposition showed 5/5 on newly introduced
items against 13/20 on carried-over items, with failure concentrated
precisely where the note is silent on the tested distinction and near-absent
where it is explicit.

The generalizable claim is narrow and worth stating exactly: an extracted
study note is a sufficient but incomplete assessment substrate, and a score
computed against one is a statement about the note's coverage unless the
score is anchored to it line by line. The note's three defects and the cause
of the key's letter displacement remain open.

\section{Arithmetic Checks}
\label{sec:appendix}

All figures reported in \S\ref{sec:accuracy} and \S\ref{sec:decomposition}
are recomputable from the counts stated in the session record. The checks
below use no information beyond those counts.

\begin{align*}
\text{Nominal total}       &= 25 \times 4 = 100 \text{ points} \\
\text{W1 (strict)}        &= \frac{18}{25} = 72.0\pct \\
\text{W2 (sel.\-weighted)}&= \frac{18 + 2.25}{25} = \frac{20.25}{25} = 81.0\pct \\
\text{W3 (strict, excl.)} &= \frac{18}{25-4} = \frac{18}{21} = 85.714\ldots\pct \approx 86\pct \\
\text{Decomposition}      &= \frac{5}{5} = 100.0\pct \qquad \frac{13}{20} = 65.0\pct \\
\text{Reconciliation}     &= 5 + 13 = 18 \quad\checkmark
\end{align*}

The W2 residual of $2.25$ points over three partial items is consistent as a
total; the per-item fractions behind it were not retained and are not
reconstructed here. The W3 figure is reproduced only under the allocation in
which all four excluded items fall among the seven non-correct items, which
is the unique allocation yielding the reported value.
